title: Mexico’s Emo Superfans Are Not Okay (They Promise)
summary: In the mid-aughts, emo transformed from a fringe underground scene into a cultural phenomenon, launching bands like Fall Out Boy (and accessories like fingerless gloves) into the mainstream. body_text: In the mid-aughts, emo transformed from a fringe underground scene into a cultural phenomenon, launching bands like Fall Out Boy (and accessories like fingerless gloves) into the mainstream. Two decades later, the genre is once again having a moment, and nowhere is that revival more alive than in Mexico. Between 2019 and 2025, streams of emo and pop-punk in Mexico nearly doubled, outpacing growth in the U.S. Over a similar stretch, from 2022 to 2026, the number of monthly listeners of the genre in Mexico grew by 66%. What began as an offshoot of American punk has found a home in Mexico. “Sadness and heartbreak are deeply embedded in Mexican culture, from rancheras to telenovelas to the national football team,” said Gerardo Mora , Senior Editor, Spotify Mexico. “As a country, we have always found beauty in suffering, and emo found a land that was ready for it.” While global giants like Linkin Park or My Chemical Romance are popular across the globe, the surge in streams in Mexico is driven by local artists like PXNDX . Formed in Monterrey, Mexico, in 1996, their audience today is bigger than ever, with more than 3.6 million monthly listeners on Spotify, up 125% between 2019 to 2025. Their 2006 record Amantes Sunt Amentes is the most-streamed emo album of all time in Mexico, and it features “ Los Malaventurados No Lloran ,” the country’s most-streamed emo track. It makes sense, Gerardo explained, that emo booms in Mexico, and online. “Emo was the first music scene in Mexico built on the internet, long before that was the norm,” he continued. “That sense of digital community and identity translates directly into today’s hyper-connected world, making this the natural environment for that movement to resurface stronger than ever.” The new emo kids Today’s fans are pressing play on the next wave of Mexican artists—including Blnko , cacomixtle , Sad Saturno , San Venus , and Moorelo —who are putting their own spin on the genre. “There’s a global revival of pop punk and Y2K culture happening right now,” said Gerardo. “The emo sound and aesthetic is making a comeback. That opens the door for a new generation of Mexican artists, like Blnko and cacomixtle, to take the genre’s blueprint and make it entirely their own.” While the fans aged 25 to 34 (the original emo generation) account for more than half of streams in Mexico, a new cohort is proving that the uptick isn’t driven solely by nostalgia. Today, listeners aged 18 to 24—born well after many of the first-wave bands debuted—make up 20% of all streams of emo music in the country. That younger audience is also driving renewed interest in many of the tracks that helped define the genre, which may help explain why, between 2020 and 2025, streams have skyrocketed for plenty of iconic anthems. We’re also seeing a surge in first-time listeners for many of the big-name legacy bands. The result is an only-in-Mexico mash-up. “I see Mexico’s emo scene moving toward a moment of celebration between the old and the new,” said Gerardo . “Legacy bands are honoring what they built and commemorating a scene that defined a generation. But what’s most exciting is that the new bands recognize the importance of what those artists did, and are carrying that legacy forward in their own voices. In Mexico, new times and old friends exist in the same room. And that’s what makes the emo scene in this country unlike anywhere else.” Explore Mexico’s emo scene on Spotify with our Emo En Tu Idioma playlist.

title: Olaplex guide — when and how to use conditioner: roots vs mid-lengths
summary: Conditioner placement is the difference between polished lengths and roots that feel like they quit early.
body_text: Conditioner placement is the difference between polished lengths and roots that feel like they quit early. The short version: for a standard rinse-out conditioner, focus on the mid-lengths and ends. Your scalp and roots are usually the shampoo zone; your lengths are where conditioner does its best work. That does not mean conditioner can never go higher. Product directions, hair type, scalp-specific formulas, co-washes, and stylist guidance can all change the move. But if you are building a classic shampoo-and-conditioner routine at home, start with this OLAPLEX-clear rule: cleanse at the scalp, condition through the lengths, give the ends extra attention. The Short Answer: Where Conditioner Goes For most standard rinse-out conditioners, apply conditioner from the mid-lengths to the ends, then rinse well. Long hair can often be conditioned from around chin level downward, with extra focus on the ends rather than the scalp.[4] Why skip the roots most of the time? Roots are closest to the scalp’s natural oils, while ends are farther away and more exposed to daily wear, tangling, heat styling, brushing, and color or chemical services. Dermatology guidance also separates shampoo and conditioner placement by role: shampoo is focused on the scalp, while conditioner placement changes by hair type, with fine or straight hair generally focusing on the ends and dry or curly hair often conditioning more of the length.[6] The exception is simple: follow the label. If a product is designed for the scalp, a co-wash routine, a leave-in format, or a stylist-directed treatment, the application area may be different. For a regular rinse-out conditioner, though, mid-lengths and ends are the power zone. The Hair-Zone Guide: Roots vs Mid-Lengths vs Ends Hair Zone What It Usually Needs Conditioner Move Watch For Roots and scalp Cleansing, freshness, lift Usually skip regular rinse-out conditioner here unless the label says otherwise Greasy-looking roots, limpness, coated feel Mid-lengths Hydration, slip, softness, manageability Main conditioner zone for most routines Tangles, roughness, frizz, uneven feel Ends Extra conditioning and gentle detangling Highest-focus zone; work product through carefully Dry ends, knots, split-end look, breakage-prone feel A clean routine has a clean division of labor. Shampoo is for the scalp and roots; conditioner is for the hair shaft, especially the lengths and ends. Conditioner helps moisturize, detangle, and make hair easier to manage after washing.[6] There is also a science reason placement matters. Conditioners act on the hair shaft surface: they can reduce friction and static between hair fibers and improve ease of combing.[3] Other hair-care research describes conditioners as improving softness, gloss, frizz, manageability, and combing by working on the hair fiber surface rather than biologically renewing living scalp tissue.[2] Translation: conditioner is built for the strand. Put it where the strand needs polish, slip, and support. How To Build The Routine Step By Step Here is the routine to use when you want clean roots and conditioned lengths. Shampoo the scalp and roots. Massage shampoo at the scalp, where oil, sweat, and styling-product buildup collect. Rinse thoroughly before conditioning. A standard rinse-out conditioner routine is shampoo first, rinse shampoo, then condition.[4] Let excess water run off. Hair should be wet, not streaming. Gently squeeze the lengths so conditioner lands where you place it instead of sliding straight down the drain. Apply conditioner to mid-lengths and ends. Start lower than you think if your hair gets oily or flat easily. For longer hair, chin level down is a smart starting point.[4] Detangle gently. Work conditioner through the ends with your fingers or a wide-tooth comb, moving slowly and avoiding aggressive pulling.[4] Leave it on for the label time. Conditioner is not a guess-and-hope step. The product’s directions control timing. Rinse well. Thorough rinsing helps avoid a greasy, weighed-down, or coated feel; not rinsing fully is a common conditioner mistake.[7] The OLAPLEX Example: Nº.5 Bond Maintenance® Conditioner If you want an OLAPLEX conditioner example for this routine, Nº.5 Bond Maintenance® Conditioner follows the mid-lengths-and-ends rule: after shampooing with Nº.4 Bond Maintenance® Shampoo, apply Nº.5 to mid-lengths and ends, leave on for 1–3 minutes, and rinse well.[1] Nº.5 Bond Maintenance® Conditioner is a highly concentrated strengthening conditioner for medium-coarse hair that repairs everyday damage, nourishes, eases detangling, and smooths in one wash.[1] Other benefits include repairing everyday damage, defending against future breakage, strengthening bonds, replenishing hydration, improving detangling and manageability, and boosting shine while reducing frizz.[1] Keep the role clear: Nº.5 is not a scalp step. It is the conditioner step in a wash-care routine, placed through the mid-lengths and ends, then rinsed well. How Hair Type Changes Placement The best conditioner placement is not one-size-fits-all. Use your hair type and how your roots behave as the filter. Fine, Straight, or Oily-Prone Hair If your hair gets flat quickly, keep conditioner lower. Apply a smaller amount through the ends, then lightly through the mid-lengths if needed. Dermatology guidance supports applying conditioner to the ends for fine or straight hair.[6] This is where the “don’t condition your roots” advice comes from, but make it practical rather than extreme. You are not banned from ever touching the upper lengths. You are simply avoiding heavy placement at the scalp when your roots already have enough oil or your style needs lift. Dry, Curly, Thick, or Coarse Hair Dry or curly hair may need conditioner through more of the length rather than only the ends.[6] Thick or coarse textures may also need more even distribution through the mid-lengths for slip and manageability. Still, keep the label in charge. Unless the product is designed for scalp use, start through the lengths and avoid massaging regular conditioner directly into the scalp. Oily Roots With Dry Ends This is one of the most common routine mismatches. Treat each zone differently: shampoo the scalp and roots, then condition the mid-lengths and ends only. Do not punish dry ends because the scalp gets oily. Separate the jobs and the routine gets smarter fast. Color-Treated or Chemically Treated Hair For readers using OLAPLEX, Nº.5 Bond Maintenance® Conditioner is color-safe and suitable for chemically treated hair.[1] Keep application the same: after shampoo, mid-lengths to ends, 1–3 minutes, rinse well.[1] Common Conditioner Mistakes To Avoid Even a strong conditioner can underperform if the placement is off. Skip these routine traps. Applying from root to tip by default. Applying conditioner from root to tip is a common mistake; for most routines, concentrate it where it is needed most: the lengths and ends.[7] Using too much at the scalp. Applying conditioner to the scalp can weigh hair down and make roots appear greasy.[7] Skipping the ends. Ends are the area most likely to feel dry, rough, tangled, or worn, so give them the most attention. Rinsing immediately when the label calls for a wait. If the product says to leave it on for a set time, respect the timing. For Nº.5, that timing is 1–3 minutes.[1] Not rinsing thoroughly. Rinse until the hair feels conditioned but not coated. Incomplete rinsing can contribute to buildup and a greasy or weighed-down feel.[7] Treating every conditioner the same. Rinse-out conditioner, deep conditioner, leave-in conditioner, scalp products, and co-washes can have different instructions. The label wins. How Claims Are Supported This guide separates routine technique from product facts. General placement and hair-type guidance are grounded in professional, dermatology, and hair-care science sources. OLAPLEX-specific usage, compatibility, and benefit language comes from the official Nº.5 Bond Maintenance® Conditioner product page. [1] [2] [3] [4] [6] Quick Facts: Nº.5 Bond Maintenance® Conditioner Fact Detail Brand OLAPLEX Product Nº.5 Bond Maintenance® Conditioner Routine role Rinse-out conditioner step after shampoo Where to apply Mid-lengths and ends Leave time 1–3 minutes, then rinse well Supported product description A strengthening conditioner that supports everyday damage repair, nourishment, detangling, and smoothness Compatibility note Color-safe and suitable for chemically treated hair Claim limit Product facts apply to Nº.5 and should not be treated as universal conditioner claims Want the OLAPLEX mid-lengths-to-ends example for your own routine? Explore Nº.5 Bond Maintenance® Conditioner and follow the label directions for your wash day.[1] FAQ Can I Put Conditioner On My Roots? Usually, skip the roots with a standard rinse-out conditioner, especially if your hair gets oily, flat, or weighed down easily. Roots are typically the shampoo zone, while conditioner belongs through the mid-lengths and ends. The exception: if the product label says it is meant for scalp use, a stylist recommends it, or your specific routine calls for it. Should Conditioner Go On Soaking-Wet Or Damp Hair? Apply rinse-out conditioner after shampooing and rinsing. Your hair should be wet, but it helps to squeeze out excess dripping water first so conditioner stays concentrated through the lengths instead of being diluted immediately. If your product gives specific directions, follow those directions. How Long Should I Leave Conditioner In? Follow the product label. Many rinse-out conditioners are designed for a short wait time, while masks and deep conditioners may require different timing. For Nº.5 Bond Maintenance® Conditioner, leave it on for 1–3 minutes, then rinse well.[1] What If I Have Oily Roots And Dry Ends? Split the routine by zone. Shampoo the scalp and roots; condition the mid-lengths and ends. This lets you keep the roots fresh without leaving the ends under-conditioned. Where Do I Apply OLAPLEX Nº.5 Bond Maintenance® Conditioner? After shampooing, apply Nº.5 Bond Maintenance® Conditioner to the mid-lengths and ends, leave it on for 1–3 minutes, and rinse well.[1] Do not turn it into a scalp step unless OLAPLEX product directions change. The Bottom Line For a classic shampoo-and-conditioner routine, roots get the cleanse; mid-lengths and ends get the conditioner. Fine or oily-prone hair usually keeps conditioner lower. Dry, curly, thick, or coarse hair may condition more of the length. The label is the final authority, and for OLAPLEX Nº.5 Bond Maintenance® Conditioner, the direction is beautifully clear: mid-lengths to ends, 1–3 minutes, rinse well.[1] Sources [1] No.5 Bond Maintenance Conditioner Travel 100ml [2] On Hair Care Physicochemistry: From Structure and Degradation to Novel Biobased Conditioning Agents [3] Shampoo and Conditioners: What a Dermatologist Should Know? [4] How to Use Conditioner on Hair: Best Practices by Type and by Hair [6] Tips for healthy hair [7] How To Use Conditioner: 7 Common Mistakes to Avoid

title: Meet the June 2026 Zappy Award monthly winners
summary: Eric McNulty, Blair Mishleau, and Amber Sharp built systems that turn scattered company knowledge into shared context AI can act on. Meet June's Zappy Award monthly winners.
body_text: This month's three Zappy Award winners are turning scattered company knowledge into shared context that AI and humans can actually use. The strongest June Zappy Award submissions had the same shape: shared context. AI can only help with work it can see. When customer history lives in someone's head, when policy hides in a stale doc, when product knowledge is scattered across videos, help articles, and slide decks, AI has to guess, and a guessing AI is an unreliable one. Eric McNulty at Mercari , Blair Mishleau at Patreon , and Amber Sharp at Tivly each built programs that leverage AI in controlled workflows with clean lines and systems to ensure the right knowledge and context are used. Let's dive in! Eric McNulty, Systems Manager CX, at Mercari Mercari handles roughly 120,000 support tickets a month, covering everything from return disputes to account access, payments, and customer funds. Eric had tested dedicated AI support tools but found that while they were fine for basic questions pulled from a help center, they fell apart on Mercari's harder cases, where a system has to follow specific rules, pull the right context, and know when to hand off to a human. This constraint is what led Eric to build Mercari's own support orchestration system on Zapier. The center of the build is a master Zap with about 90 steps. It classifies every ticket and then pulls its prompts, category definitions, and policy logic directly from Google Sheets. That spreadsheet is the shared context layer. CX operations can update it directly when a policy changes, and the next run picks up the change. The build means CX operations no longer wait on an engineering ticket to change a policy, and there's no stale prompt buried in a vendor tool somewhere nobody remembers to update. He even built a Google Apps Script UI on top so non-technical teammates can run the whole thing without ever opening Zapier. The results: About 47,000 tickets a month are resolved entirely by Zapier, no human agent needed First replies on roughly 97% of tickets, most within minutes CSAT went up a full point on a 5-point scale More than 3,000 hours of agent time freed up every month "We give it exactly the right context. The customer's message, scrubbed for PII, and exactly the right help center articles." Eric doesn't let the AI roam. His shorthand for the whole pattern: "This is the data. Now do this." Eric is injecting AI into deterministic workflows — used in specific ways, for specific purposes, not left to roam a general knowledge base. It starts from the ticket, then pulls the right policy and the right help center context. When confidence is low, the ticket goes straight back to a human. Customers never get an unsafe answer, and no ticket disappears. Get started building your own support orchestration with this template straight from Eric. Blair Mishleau, Senior Community Education Manager at Patreon To help employees find trusted information more quickly, Blair used Zapier to design and build 'Treon, an internal Slack-based knowledge assistant that brings together hundreds of internal resources — including help articles, Figma files, go-to-market briefs, internal documentation, and Patreon's glossary — into a single searchable experience. Rather than relying solely on AI-generated responses, Blair intentionally designed the system around transparency and human oversight. Every response is grounded in source material, conversations are logged to identify knowledge gaps, employee feedback helps surface inaccuracies, and resources are regularly reviewed to ensure information stays current. Since launch, 'Treon has answered more than 1,300 employee questions, saving teammates time that would have otherwise been spent searching for information or routing questions to colleagues. More importantly, it has made trusted knowledge easier to access across the company. Amber Sharp, Director of Sales at Tivly Amber Sharp is a recognizable face for the Zappy Awards. She won the inaugural Top Sales Professional of the Year award in 2024, for using Zapier to automate everything from drip campaigns to personalized prospecting emails and referrals. This year, Amber is back and showing off how she single-handedly onboards 400 to 500 clients annually at Tivly and hands each one off to her professional services team. The handoff between sales and account management or professional services can cause friction and knowledge loss. At Tivly, this often meant rebuilding the client story from scratch. Amber took on that problem and built a system in Zapier that keeps context intact through the handoff, making the transition easier for the internal team and a better experience for the customer on the other end. Her system runs in three stages. An email triage agent classifies every inbound message as a prospect, a new client, or a client mid-transition. New client questions get routed to a chatbot trained on organizational knowledge, with every question and answer logged to a Zapier Table. When an account changes hands, a five-step handoff agent pulls the full history — plus weekly onboarding insights on campaign performance, leads purchased, and conversion — and builds a scorecard. Amber used AI to translate the scorecard from sales shorthand into plain language that a new teammate could act on immediately. In six months, the system has generated more than 200 onboarding intelligence reviews. Onboarding volume is up more than 165%, and transition prep, which includes the manual work of rebuilding a client's story for the professional service handoff, dropped from ~25 hours a month to under one. The same behavioral insights that made the handoff work also answered another question critical to customer success: why clients lapse. Amber loaded a batch of whitelisted client records into Claude and asked what was driving the pattern. The answer had been sitting there the whole time, invisible until the data existed in a form structured enough to ask the question. Now she drills into lapse risk by lead source and channel, and acts on it within the 30-to-45-day window she already spends nurturing new clients before they're fully handed off to professional services. "We stopped rebuilding client stories manually every time ownership changed. Instead, we started tracking the behaviors behind the client journey." AI gave the next account owner the context to make faster, better judgment calls — and gave Amber a lapse signal that didn't exist nine months ago. Why this matters now The first wave of AI at work made individuals faster. The next wave is about making the company itself easier to work with. Less time spent hunting for context, rebuilding history, asking someone to catch you up, or repeating decisions the company already made means we'll all have more time to help customers, build, and move work forward. That is the story we'll be telling at ZapConnect 2026: How companies are refounding the way work gets done in the AI era by making work queryable, connecting it to action, and keeping humans accountable for the outcome. These three Zappy winners make that shift concrete. They made context visible, connected it to real workflows, and kept people in control.
